subject: SpectralAI - footprint & quantization tradeoffs for Dedicated pool
messages:
From: Lisa Park <lisa.park@spectralai.com>

Subject: Dedicated capacity ask + workload profile attached

Hi Markus,

Thanks again for the demo last week. We liked Redwood's routing and the canary rollback behavior — that's a must for our platform team. We're moving a high-throughput inference workload into production and evaluating reserved capacity for predictable latency and data isolation.

Attached is a first-pass workload profile (QPS per model variant, typical context distribution, and representative request/response sizes). High level: two models in production (spec-legacy-16k, spec-v2-32k) with a steady state of ~45 tps combined and 95th percentile peak bursts up to ~120 tps for a few minutes. Average request sequence length is ~1.2k tokens, but the 95th is closer to 18k for longer multi-turn sessions.

Questions for you:
- What reserved GPU footprint should we expect for an initial Dedicated pool to meet 99th%-ile latency targets (<=200ms token latency)?
- How much does switching spec-v2-32k from fp16 to 4-bit/QLoRA-style quantized variants change the GPU count?
- If we enable aggressive KV prefix caching (per-request prefix reuse ~30%), how much headroom does that buy?

We're on a tight timeline — deciding on a 6–12 month committed pool by end of May. Can we get a short sizing recommendation and a mutual action plan?

Thanks,
Lisa
Lisa Park
Director, Platform Engineering | SpectralAI

Lisa — thanks for the profile, that helps. I skimmed the CSV and pulled a couple of quick back-of-envelope numbers before we do a deeper sizing exercise.

Short answer up front: for your stated steady-state (45 tps) and a 99th%-ile token latency target of ~<=200ms, a conservative starter Dedicated pool would be in the 6–8 GPU range on A100/80GB-class hardware for fp16 model variants. If you quantify spec-v2-32k down to a production-grade 4-bit variant with verified quality retention, you could see that drop to ~4–5 GPUs because of the reduced memory footprint and higher packing per device.

Key assumptions I used:
- spec-legacy-16k active shard memory (fp16 w/ KV caching) ~42GB resident per model instance; spec-v2-32k (fp16, full KV) ~85GB.
- With 30% prefix reuse, effective per-request KV traffic reduces ~20–25% in throughput-limited scenarios.
- We assume ~2x dynamic batch multiplier under burst (continuous batching) without violating latency SLOs due to your ~200ms token target.

Open items we should confirm in a short follow-up:
1) Model sizes and whether your team is comfortable with a QLoRA/4-bit variant for spec-v2-32k in production. We need evals on hallucination/accuracy delta at that precision.
2) Typical session stickiness & token emission distribution (you provided 95th request length but distribution shape matters for batching).
3) Desired SLA for regional failover (single-region vs multi-region).

I'll loop Rishi for detailed memory math and Karthis for workload-shaping / autoscaling policy input. Can we schedule a 45-min sizing call tomorrow?

—Markus
Markus Klein
Senior Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
From: rishi_malhotra@redwood.ai

Following up with concrete numbers and a simple table (inline) — conservative sizing first, then reduced-count scenarios with quantization and caching.

Assumptions called out: batch size tuned for 200ms token latency, continuous KV cache with prefix reuse=30%, work measured in contextual memory and KV working set. Model memory numbers are resident GPU peak per model when serving both weights (quantization-dependent) and KV cache (for 32k context).

Conservative (fp16 variants):
- spec-legacy-16k: peak resident ~42GB -> 1 instance per GPU on A100-80GB (with small headroom); throughput per GPU ~= 8–10 tps (real-world with batching & rpc overhead)
- spec-v2-32k: peak resident ~85GB -> requires either 2 GPUs per instance (model-sharded) or larger memory instances; throughput per 2-GPU instance ~= 10–14 tps

Result: to support 45 tps steady + 20% operational buffer -> ~6 GPUs (if we colocate and mix smaller 16k instances and split the 32k across 2 GPUs) and plan for burst headroom (we recommend 2 additional GPUs for safety) -> total 8 GPUs.

Quantized (4-bit production-grade) for spec-v2-32k:
- quantization lowers weight memory ~2.5–3x (so 85GB -> ~30GB resident), plus KV stays similar unless we compress it. That means spec-v2-32k could run as single-instance per GPU similar to 16k footprint.
- throughput per GPU increases because more batch packing possible — realistic 14–18 tps per GPU.

Result: same SLA target with 4-bit quantized spec-v2-32k + 30% prefix cache reuse -> ~4 GPUs base, 5 GPUs with operational buffer.

Caveats and operational notes:
- Engineering validation: need quantized evals (regression set and holdout prompts) to validate quality. Our Optimize team can run a systematic eval suite and produce automated alerts on regressions.
- KV compression: if you can tolerate lossy KV compaction or compression, KV memory drop gives even more headroom (another ~15–20% reduction).
- Canary & fallback: recommend a canary policy that pins a small percentage of traffic to fp16 variant while quantized runs majority traffic; automatic fallback if quality drift detected.

Attachments: I can share a quick spreadsheet that maps tps -> GPUs under each scenario, and a mutual action plan template for procurement timelines.

—Rishi
